I'm 65 now, and I've farmed these 20 mu in Quzhou for 30 years. My household has seven mouths — my wife, my son and his wife, their two children, and my younger daughter who helps when she's not at her factory job. With some of them working outside, we have a bit of cash, but I'm still careful. Fertilizer and diesel for the well pump aren't getting any cheaper.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October. I planted 16 mu with an improved variety — I don't remember the exact name, but it's the one I've used for five years now, the one that doesn't lodge too bad. This spring, I'll topdress with urea when it turns green. In total I use about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu — the extension agent says 15, but I add a bit more because I'd rather waste a little money than lose yield. I also put down compound fertilizer as basal, so I get some phosphorus and potassium too, about 6 and 5 kg per mu. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter freeze-up, once in March when the wheat greens up, and once at jointing if the rain is short. For chemicals, I spray herbicide once in early spring and insecticide twice — that's three applications total. I rotary tilled before planting last autumn. If the weather holds, I expect about 450 kg per mu.

Summer maize gets planted right after wheat harvest in mid-June. There's barely a week between harvest and planting, so I plant no-till directly into the wheat stubble — everybody does it that way, there's no time to till. I buy hybrid seed every year, about 14 kg nitrogen per mu total with compound at planting and urea at the big trumpet stage, plus a little phosphorus and potassium. I'll irrigate twice if it's dry, and spray three times — herbicide once and insecticide twice for corn borer. I usually get about 500 kg per mu.

I keep 4 mu for chrysanthemum. It's my cash crop — the medicine buyer pays decent money for dried flowers. I plant seedlings in late April after rotary tilling. Chrysanthemum needs more attention than grain: I give it about 18 kg nitrogen per mu, plus phosphorus and potassium, irrigate three times, and spray four times because aphids and mildew always come. Yield is usually around 140 kg per mu of dried flowers.

I manage it this way because wheat and maize are my foundation — they feed the family and provide straw for the animals. The chrysanthemum is where I earn cash for school fees and medicine. At my age, I don't experiment anymore. I do what worked last year, and I watch my neighbors. If Lao Wang's wheat looks better, I'll ask him what he did, but I won't change much.
